summary: A proposal from John Davidson, Will Crowther, John McConnell and Jon Postel describing an echoing strategy for terminals connected over satellite links. Because each character must travel to the server and back, echo can feel sluggish, with delays of nearly half a second or more. The note outlines why this is a problem and how echoing might be organized to reduce it. It builds on RFC 346.

plainLanguage.summary: When you type a letter and it only shows up after a long wait, typing feels weird. This note suggests ways to show your letters faster even when the signal travels far.

subtitle: A proposal to hide satellite delay by letting the user's TELNET echo typed characters under server control.

tldr.problem: Over a satellite link, each typed character must travel to the server and back before it is echoed, so latency between keying and printing is nearly half a second, and echo delays of at least one second are expected to be common.
tldr.mechanism: With Remote Controlled Echoing (RCE), the server tells the user-side TELNET in the TIP which characters are breaks and when to echo, discard or print server output, so echo happens locally.
tldr.outcome: It is a proposed optional addition to User TELNET; the next step named is simulation and an experimental TELNET.

today: The unit metadata lists this RFC's status as Unknown, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC is a proposal, and its own conclusion names simulation and an experimental TELNET as the next steps.

sections.title: The Satellite Echo Problem
sections.content:
Interactive systems that echo characters for full-duplex terminals get more awkward as transmission delays grow, because a character's round trip time is added to the server's own echo delay. For a terminal separated from its server by a single satellite link, the latency between keying and printing is nearly half a second even if the server echoes instantly. Routing through part of the surface net adds more.

This RFC (see also RFC 346) describes a strategy that removes the delay of simple echoing, so the transmission delay is hidden in the cost of computation only. It is an optional addition to existing User TELNETs and needs a cooperating server process.
sections.plainLanguage: If every letter has to go to a far-away computer and back before you see it, typing feels slow. They want a way to hide that wait.

sections.title: Standard Echoing and Break Characters
sections.content:
Normally a server task called the Terminal Handler echoes each character and buffers input for the user process. The process names wakeup characters, which wake it when echoed, and break characters, which make the handler suspend echoing so a command's output response is not mixed with type-ahead. Echoing resumes once the process finishes its response.

For example, a user typing CO [ESC] ABC [ESC] XYZ should see COPY (FROM FILE) ABC (TO FILE) XYZ however fast they type. The process can also ask for no echo at all, for hiding input such as a password.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the faraway computer shows each letter as you type, but pauses the display when it has to print its own answer, so the answers stay in order.

sections.title: Remote Controlled Echoing in the TIP
sections.content:
In Remote Controlled Echoing (RCE) the server controls echoing but the User TELNET, here the TIP, performs it. A typed character is converted to its NVT equivalent and placed in both a transmission buffer and an input buffer. Exactly one of three paths is enabled at any time: DISCARD, ECHO or OUTPUT.

The server sends TELNET commands to steer this: Use RCE, Set Break Action (echo or not echo the break character), Set Break Classes (a two-byte command), Move to Break (MTB, enabling ECHO) and Delete to Break (DTB, enabling DISCARD, which hides input). The user may also ask the server to use RCE, and the server must answer YES or NO.

In a login example, LOG NAME PASSWORD [CR] is driven by MTB, MTB, DTB and then MTB again, so the password is never printed.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper box keeps your typed letters in a line. The faraway computer says 'show these', 'hide these' or 'now show my answer', and the box does it at once.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Open Issues
sections.content:
The delay becomes visible only as extra processing time at a break, and users who type ahead may notice it only at the first break. If the TIP buffers input before sending, it transmits at least at every break character, and the server should be able to ask for more frequent sending.

Unsolicited output, such as a system message, enables the OUTPUT path until an MTB or DTB or an empty output buffer re-enables ECHO or DISCARD; the RFC calls this a kludge. Eleven open issues are listed, including clearing buffers and how to echo a CR or TAB, some to be addressed in RFC 358. The conclusion does not recommend discarding current TELNET, and RCE should not be used for half-duplex devices that echo themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: It mostly works, but the authors list questions they still have and say the old way should stay available.

items.title: DISCARD
items.text: Characters leave the input buffer and are discarded.

items.title: ECHO
items.text: Characters move from the input buffer to the print buffer.

items.title: OUTPUT
items.text: Characters move from the output buffer to the print buffer.
